title: Commutes Sentence of Irving Stitsky
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Irving Stitsky as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Irving Stitsky’s federal sentence on December 23, 2020. The Justice Department lists an original term of 85 years in prison, three years of supervised release and $23,152,235 in restitution for securities, wire and mail fraud convictions in the Southern District of New York. The clemency register records the grant, but not its full terms.
description_long:
On December 23, 2020, Donald Trump commuted Irving Stitsky’s federal sentence. The Justice Department lists an original judgment from the Southern District of New York: 85 years in prison, three years of supervised release and $23,152,235 in restitution. The offenses included securities fraud, wire fraud and mail fraud. The restitution award was part of the judgment alongside the prison term, so clemency should not be read as erasing the underlying financial obligation.

A commutation grants relief from punishment while leaving the conviction in place; it is different from a pardon. The public clemency register records the original sentence and the date of Trump’s action, but does not show the exact replacement terms in the warrant. It therefore does not establish how much of the prison term was removed or whether any conditions were changed. The documented event is the presidential commutation of a sentence imposed in a securities-fraud case, with the conviction and restitution amount still listed in the federal record.

title: Commutes Sentence of Jeff Cheney
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Jeff Cheney as part of a clemency list.

Cheney had received 216 months in prison and ten years of supervised release for conspiring to manufacture and distribute methamphetamine after a prior felony drug conviction. The Justice Department’s clemency register identifies the case in Iowa and records the original judgment, but does not specify the revised sentence.
description_long:
Jeff Cheney’s federal case involved a conspiracy to manufacture and distribute at least 500 grams of methamphetamine after a prior felony drug conviction. In 2008, the Northern District of Iowa sentenced him to 216 months in prison and ten years of supervised release. Donald Trump commuted that sentence on January 19, 2021, the day before leaving office.

The Justice Department lists the original punishment and the commutation date, but its public entry does not state what sentence replaced the 216-month term. A commutation changes the punishment; it does not vacate the conviction or amount to an acquittal. The distinction matters here because the record documents relief from the sentence imposed for the drug conspiracy, while leaving the conviction itself in place. The entry also does not explain the clemency decision or specify any revised supervision requirements. Without the warrant’s terms, it is not possible to say how much prison time remained or whether other conditions changed. The established event is the commutation of Cheney’s federal sentence, not a reversal of his case.

title: Meta Announces Trump Account Reinstatement
description_short: Meta said it would restore Trump’s Facebook and Instagram accounts after the two-year suspension.
description_medium: Meta announced on January 25, 2023, that Donald Trump’s Facebook and Instagram accounts would be restored after a two-year suspension imposed following the January 6 attack on the Capitol. Meta said the suspension period had elapsed and that Trump would again be subject to its platform rules, including heightened penalties for repeat violations.
description_long:
Meta suspended Donald Trump’s Facebook and Instagram accounts after the January 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, citing the risk of further incitement. The company initially left the suspension’s duration open. In June 2021, it set a two-year period and said it would review whether the danger to public safety had diminished. On January 25, 2023, Meta announced that Trump would be allowed back on both platforms in the coming weeks.

Meta’s president of global affairs, Nick Clegg, said the company wanted the public to hear from elected officials, while also describing the original suspension as an extraordinary step taken in extraordinary circumstances. The reinstatement came with heightened penalties for repeat violations, according to Meta’s announcement. It restored Trump’s ability to publish to two large social networks, but did not exempt his posts from moderation rules. The decision reopened debate about how platforms should handle political speech after a major real-world event, and how long a private company should restrict a public figure’s access.

title: Trump Pushes 'Delilah Law' to Bar Commercial Licenses for Undocumented Immigrants

description_long:
Trump used his February 25, 2026, State of the Union address to ask Congress to pass the “Delilah Law,” which NPR described as a ban on commercial driver’s licenses for people in the country without legal status. The request appeared among a short list of specific measures he asked lawmakers to take up, alongside proposals on drug prices, congressional stock trading and proof of citizenship for voting.

The speech was a request for legislation, not a change to licensing rules already in effect. Congress would have to act before the proposal could become law, and the available account does not set out bill text, sponsors, an enforcement process or a vote schedule. It therefore establishes the policy Trump advocated and the group it would affect, but not how a ban would operate or whether lawmakers would adopt it. The distinction matters because a presidential address can announce priorities without creating a new legal restriction on its own.

The case put the company’s financial disclosures and valuation practices under judicial scrutiny. Any judgment about particular valuations or the defendants’ responsibility depends on the court’s findings, not simply on the fact that the trial began.

title: Targets Sanctuary Cities and Interior Enforcement
description_short: Signed Executive Order 13768 expanding interior enforcement and threatening federal funding for sanctuary jurisdictions.
description_medium: On January 25, 2017, Trump signed Executive Order 13768, “Enhancing Public Safety in the Interior of the United States.” It broadened immigration enforcement priorities and threatened federal funding for jurisdictions that limited cooperation with federal immigration authorities. The order put sanctuary-city policies in direct conflict with the administration’s enforcement agenda.
description_long:
Executive Order 13768 directed federal agencies to broaden immigration enforcement inside the United States and identified jurisdictions that limited cooperation with federal immigration authorities as targets for possible funding restrictions. Trump signed the order on January 25, 2017. It also set out enforcement priorities that reached beyond people convicted of serious crimes, expanding the range of noncitizens identified for removal.

The directive placed pressure on local governments that limited how their employees assisted federal immigration enforcement. Its funding provision did not itself resolve whether the executive branch could withhold particular grants; that question depended on statutory authority and later legal challenges. The order marked an early effort by the administration to tie federal resources to local cooperation on immigration. It established the administration’s policy and threatened consequences for sanctuary jurisdictions, while leaving implementation and the legality of specific funding actions to subsequent decisions.

title: Creates Schedule F to Purge Civil Service
description_short: Trump signed Executive Order 13957 creating “Schedule F,” enabling mass reclassification of civil servants.
description_medium: Trump created Schedule F through Executive Order 13957 on October 21, 2020. The new category covered federal positions involving confidential or policy-related work and gave agencies a path to reclassify some career employees. Reclassification could reduce the job protections normally attached to those civil-service posts; the order did not itself identify how many employees would be moved.
description_long:
Executive Order 13957 created Schedule F within the federal excepted service. It covered positions the administration considered confidential, policy-determining, policy-making or policy-advocating, and directed agencies to identify roles that fit those criteria. Moving a career position into the category could reduce the protections that ordinarily make civil servants less vulnerable to political dismissal.

Trump signed the order on October 21, 2020, near the end of his first term. The order authorized agencies to begin reviewing positions, but it did not name employees or show how many reclassifications were completed before the next administration took office. The policy raised concerns that a broad interpretation of “policy-related” work could bring career staff under greater political control. Schedule F was therefore a personnel mechanism with potential consequences for the independence of the civil service; its actual reach depended on agency implementation, not on the order’s creation alone.

title: Imposes Aluminum Tariffs Under Section 232
description_short: Trump issued Proclamation 9704 imposing 10 percent tariffs on aluminum imports under Section 232.
description_medium: On March 8, 2018, Trump issued Proclamation 9704, imposing a 10 percent tariff on aluminum imports under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act. The administration invoked national security as its legal basis. The measure became part of a wider dispute over steel and aluminum imports and trade policy.
description_long:
Proclamation 9704 imposed a 10 percent tariff on covered aluminum imports after a Commerce Department investigation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act. The administration said rising imports threatened national security, and Trump signed the measure on March 8, 2018. The tariff applied at the border to covered products, adding a cost for importers of aluminum used in construction, vehicles, packaging and other manufacturing.

Section 232 allows the president to adjust imports after a national-security investigation. Using it for aluminum made the tariff part of a wider debate over whether trade restrictions should serve as an economic or security tool. Importers pay the duty, while the amount passed along to manufacturers and buyers depends on supply chains and market conditions. The proclamation set the rate and the administration’s stated rationale; it did not itself establish what consumers would ultimately pay. The event was the use of a security statute to tax covered aluminum imports, with the broader economic effect depending on how businesses responded.

Reuters verified the clips were AI-generated and that no attack on Kharg Island had taken place. A separate U.S. strike involved Larak Island. The distinction matters because the post presented fabricated imagery as current military action.
description_long: Trump posted videos on August 30, 2026, depicting explosions at Iran’s Kharg Island oil terminal and suggesting the site was being destroyed. Reuters examined the footage and reported that it was generated by artificial intelligence; the depicted attack did not occur. The post also risked confusing Kharg Island with Larak Island, a different location where a real U.S. strike had taken place. The two islands are distinct, and the actual strike does not verify the imagery Trump shared. By circulating a fabricated scene in the context of an active conflict, the post blurred the line between authentic battlefield footage and synthetic content. The relevant factual distinction is straightforward: Reuters verified the video was AI-generated, and there was no attack on Kharg Island as shown. The post is evidence of Trump sharing misleading wartime imagery, not evidence that the oil terminal was struck. The date of the post is August 30; Reuters published its verification the next day.

title: Advocates file Nathan challenge to Trump's revised birthright order
description_short: Advocates file Nathan challenge to Trump's revised birthright order
description_medium: On September 28, 2026, immigrants’ rights advocates filed Nathan v. Trump, challenging the administration’s revised birthright-citizenship order from August. The complaint seeks relief for children excluded under the policy and alleges constitutional and statutory violations. Those are plaintiffs’ claims, not findings by a court. The filing is a new lawsuit, separate from earlier challenges to prior orders.
description_long: Immigrants’ rights advocates filed Nathan v. Trump on September 28, 2026, challenging the administration’s August revision to its birthright-citizenship order. The complaint seeks relief for children who would be excluded from citizenship under the revised policy and alleges that the order violates constitutional and statutory protections. The filing begins a new case; it does not establish that the administration acted unlawfully or that the plaintiffs will prevail. The claims belong to the plaintiffs and remain subject to the court’s review. The lawsuit is distinct from earlier litigation over the original order and injunctions because it targets the revised policy and its effect on children covered by the complaint. The ACLU announced the filing and made the complaint available. The immediate event is the challenge’s submission, not a ruling on the merits. Any account of the case should preserve that procedural posture and avoid presenting the complaint’s allegations as judicial findings.
